card.p: Eight looks from the studio floor, and exactly what to ask for.

card.h1: The season's idea: effort you can't see
card.p: Every look here is built to survive a week of real life — wet mornings, wool collars, no round brush.

ul.li: The shapes are recognisable — bob, shag, pixie — but worn loose rather than prescribed
Colour has moved off the uniform single shade and onto blended, dimensional placement that grows out without a line
Gloss is the common finish: a shine service makes colour read richer and hair read healthier
The trade we're making all season: more work in the chair, less work at home

card.h1: "The strongest hair right now feels designed, but not over-designed."
card.p: Adam Federico, Vice President of Technical Education, R+Co
It's the sentence we kept coming back to while building this collection.
A jaw-to-collarbone bob cut soft and slightly airy, so it tucks behind an ear and stays tucked. The opposite of the tight, tailored bob: worn-in on day one.

ul.li: Ask for: a bob with a soft, unblunt perimeter and invisible internal weight removal
Best on: straight to loose-wave hair, medium density
Home routine: air-dry, one pass with a flat iron only if you want it

card.p: Length kept, weight broken. The perimeter stays strong through the lengths while the face-framing pieces do the moving — which is what stops long layers collapsing into flat curtains by Wednesday.

ul.li: Ask for: a strong perimeter, dynamic face-framing, minimal wispy disconnection
Best on: thick or coarse hair carrying too much weight at the ends
Home routine: rough-dry upside down, no product until it's 80% dry

card.p: Wispy, flexible, and deliberately not a commitment: they sit soft across the forehead, blend into the length when you push them aside, and don't demand a blow-dry to look intentional.

ul.li: Ask for: soft, airy bangs point-cut to blend into your face-framing layers
Best on: anyone nervous about bangs — this is the lowest-risk version
Upkeep: a free fringe trim between appointments, in and out in ten minutes

card.p: A short shape cut to your own texture rather than against it, with a little imperfection left in on purpose. It's the season's clearest statement of individuality over a prescribed cut.

ul.li: Ask for: a crop shaped around your natural growth pattern and cowlicks
Best on: wave and curl, where the texture carries the shape
Home routine: a pea of cream on damp hair, fingers only

card.p: A warmer take on the root smudge: dimensional brunette underneath, a soft spiced tone melted through the root zone. Warm without tipping copper, dimensional without needing to be blonde.

ul.li: Ask for: a dimensional base with a warm root smudge melted through
Why it's here: it's the answer to clients who want richness but are done with high-maintenance brightness
Grow-out: softens rather than lines up

card.p: Between blonde and brunette, muted gold with a whisper of ash — the wardrobe-neutral of hair colour. Built with a seamless lift and a colour melt over the top, never a foil line.

ul.li: Ask for: "a seamless lift and a colour melt" — the phrase your colourist wants to hear
Best on: natural level 6–7 who want lighter without going blonde
Note: nowhere near green, despite the name

card.p: Our most-booked service of the season, and the shortest. A zero-lift acidic glaze over a natural dark base replaces summer's brassy ends with depth and shine — no lightener, no commitment.

ul.li: Ask for: a demi or acidic gloss to refine, not change, your existing depth
Chair time: shorter than a cut — it's the easiest yes on the menu
Pairs with: tone-on-tone colour drenching for low-contrast dimension

card.h1: 08 — Champagne Blonde, With the Money Piece
card.p: A warm, luminous blonde between platinum and golden, carrying peach and honey. The two brighter face-framing pieces do most of the visual work — the highest-impact, lowest-commitment change on the menu.

ul.li: Ask for: champagne toning plus a face-frame matched to your skin tone, not maximum lift
Pair with: a shadow root so the grow-out stays seamless

card.h1: What each look actually costs you in time
card.p: The honest version, so nobody books a colour they can't maintain. Our studio's own guidance — ask us to adjust it to your hair.

card.p: The consultation goes better when we can see the edges of what you want. What actually helps us:

ol.li: One photo you love — and one you don't, which tells us more
Your real mornings: how many minutes, and which tools you own
Your last two years of colour, including the box dye — it changes what's possible today

card.p: We'll tell you honestly if a look needs two appointments to get right.
Fifteen minutes, no charge, no obligation to book a service on the day.

p.i: Lune & Ash is a fictional salon created for this sample lookbook. All imagery is concept photography, not photographs of client work, and the looks, pricing guidance, team and contact details are illustrative examples rather than a real business.

brief.instruction: Fashion-magazine caption voice: confident, concrete, and physical. Short declarative sentences about hair, hands, mornings and weather — never marketing adjectives ("stunning", "gorgeous", "transformative") and never salon-brochure filler. Density: about 40 words per card. The template holds median 19 words per card, p90 65, so 40 is the budget for a look card and 65 is the ceiling only on the two text-forward cards (the consultation card and the upkeep card). Cover, chapter dividers and the quote card stay far under — a chapter divider is its title alone. Each look card follows the same structure so the collection reads as a set: a display number and the look's name as the heading, one or two sentences of editorial description, then the short "ask for / best on / home routine" spec lines. Keep the spec labels terse and parallel across all eight looks. Write for a salon client, not a stylist: technique names (colour melt, root smudge, acidic gloss, shadow root, money piece) appear because clients now use them when booking, but each one is explained in plain language the first time it lands. Structure rules: vary sentence length; no "Bold term: explanation" paragraph lists outside the designated spec lines; no signposting ("Let's take a look at"); no sweeping opener or inspirational closer; no "not just X — it's Y" constructions; no em dashes in body copy beyond the spec-line separators already in the outline.

This is a lookbook: the photography is the content and the words are captions on it. Give every look card a single large photograph — full-bleed or near-full-bleed — with the caption copy held on an opaque paper or lacquer plate beside or beneath it, never floating over a face. Use the template's full-bleed and photo-spine compositions heavily, and let the two chapter dividers be almost entirely image with a numeral and a title. Imagery is concept beauty photography, generated for this lookbook: editorial hair portraits in warm practical light, deep wine-red and cream harmony, shallow depth of field, natural grain, decisive off-center framing. Shoot each look from the angle that shows its point — the bob from a three-quarter turn showing the perimeter, the shattered layers in movement, the cloud bangs straight-on, the crop from behind and above, the colour looks in raking light that reads tone and dimension. Vary crop and distance across the eight so the run doesn't read as a photo grid: mix full portraits, tight nape and hairline details, and one hands-in-hair studio moment. No logos, no legible text in images, no stock-photo smiles, no teal-orange grading, no before-and-after pairings. These are concept images, so they must never be captioned or implied to be photographs of real clients or real salon work. The upkeep card is the one piece of data furniture: a hairline-ruled table in the template's style, not a chart. Give the quote card the template's three-zone quote treatment with a working-hands photograph across the middle.

Lune & Ash is an invented salon used as a coherent worked example because no real salon data, client assets or photographs were supplied. Keep the invention internally consistent throughout: one salon, one Autumn/Winter 2026 collection, one address, one voice. The disclosure line on the final card is required and must be reproduced in substance: it states that the salon is fictional, that the imagery is concept photography rather than client work, and that the upkeep guidance, team and contact details are illustrative. Keep it visible but quiet — small italic type at the foot of the card. Do not add invented awards, client testimonials, review scores, stylist biographies, follower counts, prices or booking statistics anywhere in the deck. The upkeep intervals are presented as the studio's own guidance, not as research findings, and must stay framed that way. The trend claims cited in the outline are drawn from real published reporting and must survive to the finished cards with their meaning intact: do not sharpen a hedged claim into a statistic, and do not attribute a technique to Lune & Ash that the outline attributes to the wider season.
